vignette:
Mark, 37, sits hunched slightly, his gaze often drifting to the window, a familiar pattern over the past few sessions. He’s a database administrator, a man whose life before was defined by logic, order, and the meticulous management of vast digital information. He used to find immense satisfaction in a perfectly optimized query, a clean dataset, a system running without a single error. Now, his own internal system feels irrevocably corrupted.

His world fractured eighteen months ago. It started innocently enough, a persistent cough that he, ever the pragmatist, initially dismissed as a lingering cold. Within days, it escalated into something far more sinister. The memory of gasping for air, the terrifying realization that his lungs were failing, is still vivid. He remembers the ambulance ride, the flashing lights, the frantic voices of the paramedics, all a blur of overwhelming sensory input as his body betrayed him. He was intubated in the ICU, placed on a ventilator, his life hanging by a thread due to a severe viral pneumonia that morphed into acute respiratory distress syndrome.

For weeks, he drifted in and out of consciousness, a prisoner in his own failing body. He recalls fragments: the incessant beeping of monitors, a symphony of alarms that still echo in his mind; the chilling sensation of the breathing tube down his throat, a constant chokehold; the cold, sterile smell of the hospital, clinging to him even now. There were moments of sheer terror, waking up partially sedated, unable to move, unable to speak, convinced he was suffocating. He remembers the nurses, their faces kind but distant, their voices muffled, like he was underwater. He was told later he nearly didn't make it. His ex-wife had offered some perfunctory support during the initial hospitalization, but their split had been final two years prior, leaving him largely alone to navigate the recovery.

Discharged after a grueling six weeks, Mark returned to an apartment that felt alien, his body a stranger. He was weak, emaciated, and the simple act of walking to the kitchen left him breathless. The physical scars faded, but the invisible ones deepened. He tried to return to his old routines, to the comforting predictability of his job. At first, the focused work of debugging code and optimizing databases offered a fleeting distraction. But the calm never lasted.

The nightmares started almost immediately. He wakes in a cold sweat, gasping, convinced the breathing tube is back, that he’s drowning in his own lungs. Sometimes, he’s back in the ICU, the alarms blaring, the sense of impending doom suffocating him. During the day, certain sounds – a faint beeping from a device in a colleague’s cubicle, the hiss of an air conditioning vent – can instantly transport him back to the hospital, his heart pounding, his palms sweating. He finds himself checking his pulse, his breathing, constantly monitoring his body for any sign of illness, any deviation from what he perceives as normal. He’s hypervigilant, scanning his environment, always on edge.

He avoids anything that reminds him of the trauma. He can’t watch medical dramas; the sight of an IV drip or a ventilator on screen sends a jolt of panic through him. He takes circuitous routes to work to avoid driving past the hospital district. He struggles to talk about his illness, feeling a knot tighten in his stomach whenever anyone asks how he's really doing. He finds himself isolating more, declining invitations from the few friends he still sees, preferring the solitary safety of his apartment. The thought of being vulnerable, of anyone seeing him as "weak" or "damaged," is unbearable.

His once sharp focus at work is now fragmented. He struggles to concentrate on complex coding tasks, his mind wandering, replaying snippets of his time in the ICU. He makes uncharacteristic errors, something that deeply frustrates him, as he prides himself on precision. He’s irritable with colleagues, snapping at minor interruptions, feeling a simmering anger just beneath the surface. He knows it’s not fair to them, but he can’t seem to control the outbursts. He used to love solving intricate problems, but now, the world feels like an unsolvable problem, a system with too many variables and no logical way to find a fix. He sees his own body as a corrupted database, full of errors he can’t debug, and the once comforting order of his life has been replaced by a chaotic, unpredictable fear.
